cls: Antineoplastic - oral multitargeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor (ALK/ROS1/MET)
pharm: Orally bioavailable small-molecule inhibitor of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), ROS1, and MET (hepatocyte growth factor) receptor tyrosine kinases; blocks constitutive signaling driven by ALK fusions/rearrangements and ROS1 rearrangements, inhibiting downstream proliferation and survival pathways in susceptible tumor cells.

summary: Crizotinib (Xalkori) is an oral kinase inhibitor that targets ALK, ROS1, and MET. In adults it is used for metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) whose tumors are ALK-positive or ROS1-positive. It is also approved for unresectable, recurrent, or refractory ALK-positive inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) in pediatric patients 1 year and older and in adults, and for relapsed or refractory systemic ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) in pediatric patients 1 year and older and young adults. The standard adult dose is 250 mg twice daily; pediatric dosing is based on body surface area. Important warnings include hepatotoxicity that can be fatal (monitor liver function tests), interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis that can be fatal, and QT interval prolongation; bradycardia, severe visual loss, and embryo-fetal toxicity also occur. In pediatric ALCL and IMT, severe gastrointestinal toxicity and reduced renal function with renal cysts have been observed. Crizotinib is a CYP3A substrate and inhibitor, so interactions with strong CYP3A inhibitors/inducers and with QT-prolonging or bradycardic drugs are clinically important.
indications: Treatment of adults with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) whose tumors are ALK-positive as detected by an FDA-approved test
Treatment of adults with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) whose tumors are ROS1-positive
Treatment of adult and pediatric patients 1 year of age and older with unresectable, recurrent, or refractory inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) that is ALK-positive
Treatment of pediatric patients 1 year of age and older and young adults with relapsed or refractory, systemic ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL)

admin: Take capsules orally twice daily with or without food and swallow them whole; do not open, crush, dissolve, or chew
If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is within 6 hours of the next dose, in which case skip it; do not take two doses at the same time
If the patient vomits after a dose, do not take an extra dose - take the next dose at the scheduled time
Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and other strong CYP3A inhibitors or inducers during treatment
Obtain liver function tests, ECG, and an ophthalmologic baseline as appropriate and monitor during therapy; interrupt, reduce, or discontinue for toxicity per label tables
moa: Crizotinib is an inhibitor of receptor tyrosine kinases including anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK), ROS1 (c-ros oncogene 1), hepatocyte growth factor receptor (HGFR, c-MET), and recepteur d'origine nantais (RON). Chromosomal rearrangements that create ALK fusion genes (or ROS1 rearrangements) generate constitutively active oncogenic kinases that drive aberrant downstream signaling through pathways such as RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT, promoting tumor cell proliferation and survival. By competitively inhibiting the ATP-binding site of these kinases, crizotinib blocks their autophosphorylation and the activation of downstream signaling, leading to reduced proliferation and induction of apoptosis in tumors dependent on ALK or ROS1 signaling. Inhibition of MET and the closely related kinases contributes to its activity and to some of its off-target effects.

absolute: Known serious hypersensitivity to crizotinib or any component of the formulation
relative: Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) - avoid use
Congenital long QT syndrome, significant QT prolongation, or uncorrected electrolyte abnormalities
Symptomatic bradycardia or concomitant bradycardic/QT-prolonging drugs
Concomitant strong CYP3A inhibitors or inducers
monitor: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, total bilirubin) for hepatotoxicity, which can be fatal
Pulmonary symptoms (dyspnea, cough, fever) for interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis
ECG (QT interval) and serum electrolytes for QT prolongation
Heart rate and blood pressure for bradycardia
Vision (visual acuity and ophthalmologic exam) for visual disorders/severe vision loss
In pediatric ALCL/IMT: gastrointestinal toxicity and renal function/renal cysts

preg: Based on its mechanism of action and findings in animals, crizotinib can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman. Verify pregnancy status in females of reproductive potential before starting. Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective non-hormonal contraception during treatment and for 45 days after the final dose, and advise males with female partners of reproductive potential to use condoms during treatment and for 90 days after the last dose. Avoid use in pregnancy unless the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: There are no data on the presence of crizotinib in human milk or its effects on the breastfed child or milk production. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed child, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 45 days after the final dose.
renal: No starting dose adjustment is recommended for mild (CrCl 60-89 mL/min) or moderate (CrCl 30-59 mL/min) renal impairment. For patients with severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) not requiring dialysis, reduce the starting dose to 250 mg orally once daily. Monitor renal function during treatment, particularly in pediatric patients treated for ALCL or IMT, in whom reduced renal function and renal cysts have been reported.
hepatic: Crizotinib can cause hepatotoxicity that may be fatal; monitor liver function tests closely. No starting dose adjustment is needed for mild hepatic impairment. For moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B), reduce the starting dose (e.g., 200 mg twice daily). Avoid crizotinib in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C). Interrupt, reduce, or permanently discontinue based on the severity of transaminase and bilirubin elevations per the prescribing information.

major: Strong CYP3A inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit juice) - increase crizotinib exposure and toxicity; avoid, or reduce crizotinib dose if unavoidable
Strong CYP3A inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) - decrease crizotinib exposure and efficacy; avoid concomitant use
QT-prolonging drugs (e.g., antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics/antiemetics) - additive risk of QT prolongation and torsade de pointes; avoid or monitor ECG closely
CYP3A substrates with narrow therapeutic index (crizotinib is a CYP3A inhibitor) - increased exposure of the substrate; avoid or monitor
moderate: Bradycardic agents (beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, clonidine, digoxin) - additive bradycardia; monitor heart rate
Moderate CYP3A inhibitors - may increase crizotinib exposure; monitor for toxicity
minor: No clinically significant interaction with drugs metabolized by other major CYP isoenzymes at clinical concentrations
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice because CYP3A inhibition increases crizotinib exposure.
interactions.alcohol: No specific drug interaction is described; limit alcohol because of additive potential for hepatic injury.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor ECG for QT prolongation and obtain serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium); correct abnormalities before and during treatment. Follow liver function tests for hepatotoxicity.

common: Vision disorders (visual impairment, photopsia, blurred vision)
serious: Hepatotoxicity with marked transaminase/bilirubin elevation (can be fatal)
Reduced renal function and renal cysts (pediatric ALCL/IMT)
rare: Torsade de pointes/serious arrhythmia from QT prolongation
emergency: New or worsening shortness of breath, cough, or fever (possible pneumonitis)
Yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, severe right-upper-quadrant pain (possible liver injury)
Fainting, severe dizziness, very slow heartbeat, or palpitations
Sudden or severe loss of vision
Severe or persistent vomiting/diarrhea with dehydration

monitoring: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, total bilirubin) at baseline, then monthly and as clinically indicated, with more frequent testing for grade 2-4 abnormalities
ECG for QT interval and serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium) at baseline and periodically, especially with QT-prolonging drugs or electrolyte disturbance
Heart rate and blood pressure for bradycardia
Pulmonary symptoms for interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis
Visual symptoms; ophthalmologic evaluation for new or worsening visual disorders or severe vision loss
Renal function and gastrointestinal toxicity, particularly in pediatric patients with ALCL or IMT
Pregnancy status in females of reproductive potential before starting
counsel: Take one capsule twice a day with or without food and swallow it whole; do not crush, chew, or open it
Report yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, severe stomach pain, nausea, or unusual tiredness right away - these may signal liver problems
Call your care team immediately for new or worsening shortness of breath, cough, or fever, which could indicate a lung problem
Tell your doctor if you feel faint, very dizzy, or notice a slow or irregular heartbeat
Report any vision changes such as flashing lights, blurred vision, or loss of sight, and avoid driving if your vision is affected
Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, tell your team about all your medicines, use effective birth control, and do not breastfeed during and for 45 days after treatment
pk: Tumor response over weeks; steady state reached within 15 days of twice-daily dosing
Mean terminal elimination half-life approximately 42 hours
Twice-daily dosing maintains continuous kinase inhibition; steady state in ~15 days
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F), with excursions permitted to 15-30 C
pearls: Hepatotoxicity can be fatal - monitor LFTs at least monthly (more often for abnormalities) and interrupt/reduce/discontinue per label criteria
Interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis can be fatal - hold for any suspected ILD and permanently discontinue if treatment-related pneumonitis is confirmed
Monitor ECG and electrolytes for QT prolongation, and heart rate for bradycardia; review concomitant QT-prolonging and bradycardic drugs
Visual disorders are very common; obtain ophthalmologic evaluation for new or worsening or severe visual loss
CYP3A substrate and inhibitor - avoid strong CYP3A inhibitors/inducers and grapefruit; reduce dose to 250 mg once daily with an unavoidable strong inhibitor
In pediatric ALCL and IMT, watch for severe GI toxicity and reduced renal function/renal cysts; pediatric dosing is body-surface-area based
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if your next dose is due within 6 hours, skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at once. If you vomit after taking a dose, do not take an extra dose - take your next dose at the scheduled time.
overdose: There is no known specific antidote for crizotinib overdose. Management consists of general supportive measures with close monitoring, including ECG monitoring for QT prolongation and bradycardia, liver function tests, and observation for pulmonary and gastrointestinal toxicity. Provide symptomatic and supportive care as clinically indicated.
